comment: The architecture assigns registries to national level but has no concept of a holder for shared objects that span organisations: a care-network record, a shared medication overview, a regional care plan. These objects have no single source system, so no participant is responsible for the whole, and in practice nobody maintains them.

public.text: The architecture assigns registries to national level but has no concept of a holder for shared objects that span organisations: a care-network record, a shared medication overview, a regional care plan. These objects have no single source system, so no participant is responsible for the whole, and in practice nobody maintains them.
public.suggestedRevision: Introduce holdership as an explicit architectural property: for every shared object crossing organisational boundaries, name a designated holder accountable for its integrity, availability and lifecycle, distinct from the participants contributing to it. Dutch chain-care information systems document the consequence of omitting this - functionally infrastructural objects existed, no party held them, and maintenance failed without any single actor being at fault.
